_note: Hand-kept list for the /deploy/ guide. scripts/build_deploy.py reads it, fetches FCDO, US State Dept and ReliefWeb updates, and writes deploy.json. Culture notes are general pointers written by us, not official advice; keep them short and check them with people who've worked there.

countries.name: Somalia
culture: Almost entirely Sunni Muslim and clan-based: know which clan dynamics affect your area, and let local staff lead introductions.
Dress conservatively; women usually cover hair and wear loose, long clothing. Men wear long trousers.
Ramadan changes working hours and the pace of everything: don't eat, drink or smoke in public during daylight.
Ask before photographing people, and never photograph security forces, checkpoints or government sites.
Somaliland has its own authorities, visa and rules: treat it as a separate operating environment.

countries.name: Ethiopia
culture: Mixed Orthodox Christian and Muslim population; fasting periods (Orthodox Lent, Ramadan) affect food and schedules.
Greetings matter: take time over them, and use titles (Ato, Weizero) until invited not to.
Ethiopia uses its own calendar and often its own clock (hours counted from dawn): confirm times twice.
Regional and ethnic politics are sensitive; avoid discussing them in public.
Don't photograph military, police, bridges or government buildings.

countries.name: Eritrea
culture: Foreigners need permits to travel outside Asmara; carry them and expect checkpoints.
Politics and the government are not discussed openly; don't put local contacts in a difficult position.
Roughly half Christian, half Muslim: dress modestly, especially outside Asmara.
Photography of anything official or military is likely to get you detained.

countries.name: Djibouti
culture: Mostly Muslim, with French and Somali/Afar influences; French and Arabic are official, Somali and Afar widely spoken.
Heavy foreign military presence: don't photograph bases, port areas or uniformed personnel.
Afternoons slow down in the heat and for khat; plan meetings for the morning.
Dress modestly away from hotels and the beach.

countries.name: Kenya
culture: Greetings and handshakes are important; take time before getting to business.
Coast and north-east are more conservative and largely Muslim: dress and behave accordingly there.
Single-use plastic bags are banned and the fines are real.
Never photograph police, military or government buildings; ask before photographing people.

countries.name: Sudan
culture: Many agencies now work from Port Sudan; weather here is for Port Sudan, not Khartoum.
Conservative Muslim society: modest dress for everyone, no public displays of affection, alcohol is illegal.
Travel and photography permits are needed and checked; carry copies of everything.
Hospitality is a big part of life: accept tea when offered and don't rush the conversation.

countries.name: South Sudan
culture: Mostly Christian with strong traditional and ethnic identities; ethnic politics are sensitive.
Photography is restricted and you may need a permit: don't photograph officials, soldiers or infrastructure.
Movement outside Juba is often controlled by curfews and checkpoints; follow your organisation's movement rules.
Greet people properly and show respect to elders and chiefs.

countries.name: Uganda
culture: Polite greetings are expected before any request.
Same-sex relations are criminalised with severe penalties; LGBT+ staff should take advice before travelling.
Dress is more relaxed in Kampala than in rural or Muslim areas.
Don't photograph government buildings, police or military.

countries.name: Morocco
culture: Criticism of the King or the monarchy, and of Morocco's position on Western Sahara, can be prosecuted.
Modest dress outside resorts; cover shoulders and knees in medinas and rural areas.
During Ramadan don't eat, drink or smoke in public in daylight.
Non-Muslims generally can't enter mosques (Hassan II in Casablanca is an exception).

countries.name: Algeria
culture: Travel in the south and border areas often needs an escort and permission; check with your security lead.
Conservative Muslim society: dress modestly and avoid public displays of affection.
French is widely used in business alongside Arabic.
Don't photograph police, military or government sites.

countries.name: Tunisia
culture: More relaxed than much of the region, but dress modestly outside tourist areas.
Military zones along the Algerian and Libyan borders are off limits without permission.
Ramadan affects working hours; be discreet eating and drinking in daylight.
French and Arabic are both used in business.

countries.name: Libya
culture: Control is split between rival authorities and armed groups; who controls a checkpoint matters.
Alcohol is illegal. Dress conservatively and avoid public displays of affection.
Photography of anything security-related can lead to detention.
Tribal and family links are central to doing business; relationships come first.

countries.name: Egypt
culture: Drones need prior permission and are often confiscated at the airport.
Don't photograph military sites, police, bridges or government buildings.
Dress modestly outside resorts; cover shoulders and knees, and women cover hair in mosques.
Public criticism of the government, including online, carries real risk.

countries.name: Israel
culture: Expect thorough security questioning at entry and exit, especially if you've travelled in the region.
Shabbat (Friday sunset to Saturday sunset) shuts down much public transport and business.
Dress modestly in religious neighbourhoods and at holy sites.
Learn the shelter and alert procedures where you're staying on day one.

countries.name: Palestine
culture: Access to Gaza and many parts of the West Bank is controlled by Israeli authorities and needs coordination.
Mostly Muslim with Christian communities: dress modestly and respect prayer times.
Expect checkpoints; carry ID and permits at all times.
Ask before photographing people, and never photograph checkpoints or security forces.

countries.name: Lebanon
culture: A mix of religious communities, each with its own areas and sensitivities; dress and behaviour vary by neighbourhood.
Evidence of travel to Israel can get you refused entry.
Don't photograph military, Hizballah sites or checkpoints.
Lebanese hospitality is generous: expect coffee and long conversations.

countries.name: Syria
culture: Control and rules differ by area; follow your organisation's local guidance on movement.
Mostly Muslim with significant Christian, Alawite, Druze and Kurdish communities: dress modestly and avoid sectarian topics.
Unexploded ordnance and mines are widespread: stay on known-safe routes.
Photography of anything military or official can lead to detention.

countries.name: Jordan
culture: Criticism of the King and royal family is a criminal offence.
Dress modestly outside upmarket parts of Amman and at religious sites.
Friday is the main day off; Ramadan cuts working hours.
Avoid the border areas with Syria and Iraq unless your work requires it.

countries.name: Iraq
culture: Federal Iraq and the Kurdistan Region have different entry rules and authorities.
Explosive hazards remain across former conflict areas: stick to cleared routes.
Conservative society, especially in the south: modest dress, no public displays of affection.
Tribal and religious leaders carry weight; let local staff guide introductions.

countries.name: Iran
culture: British and dual British-Iranian nationals face a significant risk of arbitrary detention.
Strict dress code in public: women must cover hair and wear loose clothing; men avoid shorts.
Alcohol is illegal. Don't photograph government or military sites, or protests.
Online activity can be monitored; be careful what you post or carry on devices.

countries.name: Saudi Arabia
culture: Alcohol and drugs are illegal, with severe penalties; some prescription medicines need approval.
Dress modestly; abayas are no longer required for foreign women but modest dress is expected.
Friday is the main day off and prayer times close some shops briefly.
Public criticism of the state or religion, including online, is prosecuted.

countries.name: Yemen
culture: Control is split between the Houthis in the north and the government and others in the south; rules and risks differ.
Very conservative society: full-length modest dress, and men and women mix little in public.
Khat chewing sessions in the afternoon are where a lot of business happens.
Landmines and unexploded ordnance are a major hazard across front-line areas.

countries.name: Oman
culture: Generally relaxed and welcoming, but conservative: cover shoulders and knees in public.
Alcohol only in licensed hotels and venues.
Don't photograph military sites, or people without asking.
Ramadan: no eating, drinking or smoking in public during daylight.

countries.name: United Arab Emirates
culture: Strict laws on drugs (including traces in blood), some prescription medicines, and offensive gestures or swearing, including online.
Cohabiting and public displays of affection can still cause problems; be discreet.
Dress modestly in malls and public areas.
Photographing people without permission, or government sites, is an offence.

countries.name: Qatar
culture: Alcohol only in licensed venues; being drunk in public is an offence.
Cover shoulders and knees in public places.
Some prescription medicines are controlled; check before you travel.
Criticism of the state or religion online is prosecuted.

countries.name: Bahrain
culture: More relaxed than some Gulf states, but modest dress is expected away from hotels.
Avoid political gatherings and demonstrations.
Don't photograph military, police or government sites.
Ramadan rules on public eating and drinking apply.

countries.name: Kuwait
culture: Alcohol is completely illegal.
Dress modestly in public.
Unexploded ordnance from 1990-91 is still found in the desert; don't pick up anything metal.
Criticism of the Emir is a criminal offence, including on social media.
